explanations.explanation: Glad is exactly the word. David says, "I was glad when they said to me, 'Let us go to the house of the LORD.'" Nobody had to drag him there. I think that's the kind of gladness you can see from across the room, like a baker when the oven timer dings on a good batch.

Not afraid, friend. David says, "I was glad when they said to me, 'Let us go to the house of the LORD.'" The invitation made him happy, not nervous. Nothing in the verse says he was shaking in his sandals, or in his gold base, if he had one.
Not unsure at all. David says right out, "I was glad when they said to me…" There's no pause, no "let me check my calendar." He heard the invitation and gladness came first.
The gates of Jerusalem, yes. David says, "Our feet are standing in your gates, O Jerusalem." They had made it all the way there. I bet those feet were happy to stop walking for a second.

Joppa is a seaside town, but that's not where David puts them. He says, "Our feet are standing in your gates, O Jerusalem." The song is about arriving at the city, not the beach. Wrong shoreline, friend, bring the towel back.

explanations.answer: At the foot of Mount Sinai
explanations.explanation: Mount Sinai is a real mountain in the Bible, where Moses, Israel's leader, met with God (Exodus 19:20). But this song isn't standing there. David says, "Our feet are standing in your gates, O Jerusalem." That's a whole different destination.
Careful, this one flips it around. David doesn't say split apart. He says, "Jerusalem is built up as a city united together." United is the word, friend, the opposite of split.
False is right. David says, "Jerusalem is built up as a city united together." So the city is joined up, not split apart. A cookie broken in half is a sad thing, but that's not this city.

True. David says the tribes go up "to give thanks to the name of the LORD." That's the reason the song gives for the trip. They're coming with thankful hearts, and I think that's a good reason to travel.

This one's actually true. The song says the tribes go up "to give thanks to the name of the LORD." So thanks is the reason given for the trip. Easy to doubt when it sounds so simple, but the text says it plainly.

Judgment is the word. David says, "For there the thrones of judgment stand, the thrones of the house of David." These are thrones tied to David's house. Sit in one of those and you'd better know what you're doing.

Glory sounds shiny and right, but it's not the word here. David says, "For there the thrones of judgment stand, the thrones of the house of David." Judgment is what the text gives. I'll admit glory would look better on a sign.

Wisdom is a lovely word, but not the one David uses. He says, "For there the thrones of judgment stand, the thrones of the house of David." The thrones are called thrones of judgment, plain and simple.
The peace of Jerusalem, yes. David says, "Pray for the peace of Jerusalem." That's the instruction, short and clear. Some instructions come with forty steps, and this one has a single line.
That's not what David says to pray for. His instruction is, "Pray for the peace of Jerusalem." The song doesn't mention enemies falling at all. It points to peace, and that's the whole request.
Rain would be nice for a farm, but it's not in this line. David says, "Pray for the peace of Jerusalem." The fields don't come up. Peace is the thing he asks them to pray for.

True. The prayer goes, "May those who love you prosper." So the first words David gives are for the ones who love Jerusalem. He hands them the words, so nobody has to stand there stuck, like me, saying "uh… good stuff… amen."
It's actually true. The prayer David gives says, "May those who love you prosper." Those who love Jerusalem are right there in the words. It's an easy one to second-guess, but the line is plain.

explanations.answer: For the sake of his brothers and friends
explanations.explanation: His brothers and friends, that's the reason he gives. David says, "For the sake of my brothers and friends, I will say, 'Peace be within you.'" It's all for them. A good line to say, and I bet it lands warmer than any "talk to you later."

explanations.answer: To win the favor of the crowds
explanations.explanation: The song never says that. David gives his reason himself: "For the sake of my brothers and friends, I will say, 'Peace be within you.'" His brothers and friends are the reason, not the crowds. I think a friend's blessing beats applause any day.

explanations.answer: Because the elders asked him to
explanations.explanation: No elders show up in this song. David says, "For the sake of my brothers and friends, I will say, 'Peace be within you.'" The reason is his brothers and friends. Nobody gave him a clipboard and an assignment.

House is the word. David ends with, "For the sake of the house of the LORD our God, I will seek your prosperity." The song began with the house of the LORD in verse 1 and finishes there too. That's a nice full circle, like a cookie box closing right at the corners.

Law isn't in that last line. David says, "For the sake of the house of the LORD our God, I will seek your prosperity." It's the house of the LORD, the same place the song started with. Law didn't make the cut.

Thrones came up earlier in the song, so it's an easy one to grab. But the last line says, "For the sake of the house of the LORD our God, I will seek your prosperity." The word is house, and it matches the very first verse.
